summary: A story of disgust, fear, and shame, in which a family's love for its provider wears into neglect and he dies of hunger, loneliness, and a rotting wound.

need-to-breathe.why: Gregor's new body breathes with a faint hiss and he draws his last breath at dawn, but breath is never a struggle.

hungry.why: Gregor finds fresh milk repulsive and rotten vegetables delicious, watches the lodgers eat while he starves, and dies hollow from refusing food.

full.why: The lodgers eat heartily while Gregor eats nothing; satiety never figures.

sleepy.why: Gregor wakes from uneasy dreams and dozes through his days under the sofa, and the father, refusing bed, sleeps every night in his uniform at the table.

nauseous.why: Fresh milk now sickens Gregor, who spits it out, and the mother is overcome at the sight of him, but no one actually retches.

dizzy.why: Gregor rocks himself off the bed with a crash, falls from the wall onto the table when his mother screams, and the mother swoons at the sight of him.

fatigued.why: Gregor opens with the exhaustion of his traveling job, the father falls asleep each night worn out by his bank job, and Gregor at the end can barely drag his dusty body.

pain.why: The father's apple lodges in Gregor's back and festers for a month, he injures a leg on the first morning, and scrapes himself bloody squeezing through the door.

disgusted.why: The family cannot bear to look at Gregor, the mother screams, the lodgers give notice, the charwoman calls him an old dung beetle, and his room fills with refuse.

itchy.why: On the first morning Gregor feels an itch on his belly, finds small white spots, and shudders at his own touch.

over-stimulated.why: Gregor hides from light under the sofa and is drawn by Grete's violin, but no sense is overwhelmed.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Rain beats on the window the first morning, but temperature troubles no one.

afraid.why: Gregor flees the father's hissing and cane, the family lives in terror of the creature in the next room, and the chief clerk bolts down the stairs.

anxious.why: Gregor frets about the train he has missed and the chief clerk at the door, and the family worries over money, the lodgers, and what to do with him.

panic.why: The chief clerk flees the apartment, the mother screams and faints when she sees Gregor on the wall, and the father chases him round the room with apples.

sensory-pleasures.why: Gregor discovers the pleasure of hanging from the ceiling and feeds happily on the rotting cheese and vegetables Grete sets out.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: Gregor creeps out to hear Grete's violin, feeling it shows him the way to the unknown nourishment he craves, and clings to his framed picture of the lady in furs.

fun-excitement.why: Gregor takes to crisscrossing the walls and ceiling for the fun of it, and once did fretsaw work in his free evenings.

love-romantic.why: Gregor recalls a cashier he courted too slowly and keeps the magazine picture of a lady in furs, and the parents end by thinking of a husband for Grete.

love-family.why: Gregor worked years to pay his father's debts, Grete feeds and cleans for him, and he dies thinking of his family with tenderness even after they cast him off.

grief.why: At Gregor's death the mother and Grete cry briefly on the father's shoulder, but relief outweighs mourning and they go out for a tram ride.

missing-someone.why: Gregor listens at the door for his family's voices and longs for his mother to visit his room, which she does only twice.

aroused-sexually.why: Gregor presses himself against the glass of the lady in furs, and the parents note at the end that Grete has grown into a pretty, shapely girl.

liking-as-a-friend.why: Gregor has no friends; he reflects that his traveling job never let him form lasting ties.

empathy.why: Grete tests which foods Gregor can eat and keeps his chair by the window, and Gregor understands his family's humiliation at taking jobs and lodgers.

compassion.why: Grete feeds and cleans for Gregor and the mother begs that his furniture be left so he can return to himself, until compassion wears out.

grateful.why: Gregor is grateful for Grete's care and notes that the family's gratitude for his years of support had long since cooled into habit.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Gregor remembers with pleasure laying his earnings on the table for his astonished family, and Grete takes early satisfaction in being Gregor's keeper.

trustful-distrustful.why: The chief clerk hints that Gregor is suspected of embezzling, and the family comes to believe Gregor would attack them if he could.

depressed.why: Shut in his room, ignored, unfed, and dusty, Gregor loses interest in everything and stops eating, dying as his family withdraws all support.

angry.why: The father drives Gregor back with a cane and bombards him with apples, and Grete finally declares with fury that the thing must go.

envious.why: Gregor envies nothing; he looks at the hospital across the street and the lodgers' dinners with longing, not envy.

jealous-friendship.why: There is no friendship to defend.

hatred.why: The family comes to hate the creature that has ruined them, the charwoman taunts him with her broom, and Grete says a human would have left of its own accord.

contempt.why: The chief clerk sneers at Gregor's excuses, the lodgers treat the family as servants, and the charwoman calls Gregor an old dung beetle.

resentment.why: Gregor rails inwardly at a boss who sits high on his desk and at a family who only used him, and the family resents the burden Gregor has become.

proud.why: Gregor once took pride in supporting the family, and the father now stands straight in his bank messenger's uniform with gold buttons.

amused.why: The absurdity of Gregor's efforts to get out of bed and the charwoman's cheerful announcement that it's croaked carry a grim comedy nobody in the story feels.

sense-of-belonging.why: Gregor is shut out of the family that gathers in the next room, and the family closes ranks against him before uniting in relief at his death.

lonely.why: Locked in his room, Gregor is visited less and less, loses even Grete, and dies alone in the dark before dawn.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Grete argues that it cannot be Gregor, because Gregor would have gone away on his own, and the family judges that they have done their duty.

admiration.why: Gregor admires Grete's playing, and the family once admired his earnings; little else earns regard.

embarrassed.why: The family is mortified before the chief clerk, then before the three lodgers who catch sight of Gregor during the violin recital.

shame.why: The family hides Gregor from everyone, the father's bankruptcy shamed them all, and Gregor hides under the sofa so his sister need not see him.

guilt.why: Gregor blames himself for ruining the family's fortunes, and the family's brief tears at his death carry a trace of guilt they quickly put away.

sad.why: Gregor weeps when the furniture is removed and when he is neglected, and the mother cries over him on her brief visits.

happy.why: The story ends with the family content on a tram in spring sunshine, planning a new flat and a husband for Grete.

joyful-euphoric.why: The family's relief when the charwoman announces Gregor is dead swells into something like joy as they take the day off and ride into the country.

effort.why: Gregor struggles for hours to get out of bed and turns the key with his jaws, and the whole family, once idle, drags itself to work.

focused-in-flow.why: No one is absorbed in a task; Gregor's days are empty and the family's jobs are drudgery.

bored.why: Gregor spends his days with nothing to do but crawl the walls and listen at the door, until even that ceases to interest him.

distracted.why: Gregor forgets himself while listening to the violin and creeps into the living room in full view.

impatient.why: Gregor races the clock to catch his train, the chief clerk demands explanations through the door, and the family grows impatient for the thing to be gone.

curious.why: Grete sets out a range of foods to learn what Gregor can eat, and the charwoman pokes him with her broom to see what he will do.

surprised.why: Gregor wakes to find himself a monstrous vermin, and each person who sees him, the chief clerk, the mother, the lodgers, is stunned.

awe.why: Nothing inspires awe; the transformation is met with horror, not wonder.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The chief clerk disbelieves Gregor's claim to be unwell, and Grete finally refuses to believe the creature is her brother.

feeling-of-knowing.why: No one strains to remember anything.

confused.why: Gregor wakes baffled by his body, his speech becomes an animal noise no one understands, and the family cannot tell whether he still understands them.

frustrated.why: Gregor cannot get out of bed, cannot make his words understood, cannot stop the furniture removal, and cannot make anyone see he is still Gregor.

uncertain-certain.why: Gregor wavers between going back to sleep and getting up, and the family debates until Grete decides that the creature must go.

understanding.why: Gregor understands from Grete's speech that he must vanish and accepts it, and the family understands at last that they are free.

inspired.why: Grete has the idea of clearing the furniture so Gregor can crawl, and the family of taking in lodgers, but insight is not the story's note.

satisfied.why: The family is satisfied that they did all they could and that their jobs are good ones, as they plan a smaller flat.

foreboding.why: The rotting apple in Gregor's back, the growing neglect, and the dust tell Gregor as well as the family where this is going.

nostalgia.why: Gregor recalls his years as the family's provider, the fretsaw evenings, and the lady in furs from a lost life.

anticipation-suspense.why: Everyone waits for Gregor to open the door on the first morning, and Gregor waits each day to learn whether Grete will still come.

hope.why: The mother hopes Gregor will come back to them, and Gregor still plans to send Grete to the conservatory at Christmas.

schadenfreude.why: The charwoman enjoys Gregor's helplessness and crows over his death.

elevation.why: Gregor's dying tenderness toward the family that discarded him is the story's one moral grace, felt by no one but him.

rage.why: The father, red-faced in his uniform, pelts Gregor with apples in a fury.
